name: Milk diet

card.summary: A monotrophic eating plan built around milk as the main or only food, used by practitioners in pursuit of a clearer complexion, weight change or general vitality.
card.note: Single-food diets can leave nutrient gaps; clinicians advise medical supervision for any restrictive plan.

quick.overview:
The milk diet is a plan in which milk supplies all or most of a person's food for a period. It has been promoted since the early twentieth century as a route to better skin, a leaner or heavier body and a general sense of well-being, which are the appearance payoffs its followers describe.

It belongs to the family of monotrophic (single-food) diets. Its best-known promoter was the physical culturist Bernarr Macfadden in the 1920s. No published trials have tested an adult milk-only plan for appearance outcomes; the research that exists on milk concerns infants, hospital feeding and ordinary dairy intake.
quick.how: Practitioners drink milk in place of meals for a set stretch of days or weeks, sometimes in large daily volumes, and some versions add other foods around it. Followers describe it as a short-term reset rather than a permanent way of eating.
quick.risks: Health writers note that single-food diets in general are associated with anaemia, bone loss, malnutrition and muscle breakdown, along with short-term constipation, diarrhoea, fatigue and low mood. Some experts also say that adopting any single-food regimen can accompany disordered eating. People who are lactose intolerant or have a milk allergy react to milk directly.

lead: The milk diet is an eating plan in which milk is the main or only food for a period of time. People who follow it generally do so for appearance-related reasons: clearer-looking skin, weight loss or weight gain, and an overall healthier look. It is classed as a monotrophic diet, meaning a diet of one food [1].

The plan was popularised in the 1920s by Bernarr Macfadden, a physical culturist who promoted milk-only regimens for conditions ranging from eczema and hay fever to impotence, reportedly calling for very large daily volumes [1]. Nineteenth-century health journals also discussed milk diets, showing the idea predates Macfadden [2].

Research on milk is extensive but concerns other populations, such as preterm infants fed exclusive human milk and adults consuming dairy as part of a normal diet. Nutrition commentary on single-food diets generally lists nutrient shortfalls as the main concern [1].

chain: Milk replaces most meals for a set period
Calorie and food-group intake change sharply
Followers report changes in weight and in how their skin looks
angle.text: Practitioners use the plan as a short-term reset, saying a simplified intake leaves them leaner (or heavier, depending on volume) and with calmer-looking skin. These are the claims made by followers; the plan has not been tested for these outcomes in adults.

paras: In its strict form the milk diet replaces meals with milk, with all calories coming from it. Looser versions treat milk as the dominant food while allowing a few additions. The approach shares its logic with other monotrophic diets: simplicity, a defined time window and a promise of a visible change [1].

Milk diets appear in medical and health literature at least as early as the 1870s, when a journal article on the subject was published [2]. In the 1920s Macfadden, a prominent figure in the American physical culture movement, promoted a milk-only regimen as a remedy for eczema, hay fever and impotence [1].
The idea persists in modern diet and fitness communities as one of several single-food plans that circulate online.

Proponents say that removing most foods lowers digestive load, supports skin clarity and produces rapid change in body weight. Different followers aim in opposite directions, some for fat loss and others for weight gain through high milk volumes.

Commentary on monotrophic diets lists anaemia, osteoporosis, malnutrition, nutrient toxicities and muscle breakdown as potential consequences of single-food eating, and notes short-term effects such as constipation, diarrhoea, fatigue and worsened mood [1].
Some experts add that pursuing any single-food diet may signal a developing eating disorder [1].

No studies found. Trials of exclusive human-milk diets exist for preterm infants, and trials of dairy milk as part of adult diets exist, but they address different questions from an adult milk-only plan.

timeline.event: A health journal publishes an article titled "Milk Diet" [2].
Bernarr Macfadden popularises a milk-only regimen [1].
